tricks.title: Making 10
tricks.method: Take 2 from the 5 to make the 8 into 10, leaving 3. 10 + 3 = 13.
tricks.why: Ten is the easiest number to add to - breaking one number apart to complete the other to 10 turns an awkward sum into two easy ones.

tricks.title: Compensation
tricks.when: Adding a number close to a multiple of 10
tricks.method: Round 29 up to 30 (add 1), calculate 47+30=77, then subtract the 1 back: 76.
tricks.why: Rounding to a friendly number makes the calculation instant; you just have to remember to undo the rounding afterward.

tricks.title: Left-to-right addition
tricks.method: Add hundreds first (200+100=300), then tens (30+50=80), then ones (4+2=6). Combine: 386.
tricks.why: Working from the biggest place value down matches how we naturally think about size, and avoids holding 'carry' numbers in your head.

tricks.title: Count up (the shopkeeper's method)
tricks.method: Count up from 77 to 82: that's 5. So 82 − 77 = 5.
tricks.why: When two numbers are close, it's often faster to find the gap between them than to subtract directly.

tricks.title: Round and compensate
tricks.when: Subtracting a number close to a multiple of 10
tricks.method: Round 19 up to 20 (subtract 20 instead): 63−20=43. Since you subtracted 1 too many, add 1 back: 44.
tricks.why: Subtracting a round number is easy; the compensation step corrects for the small amount you over-subtracted.

tricks.title: Break into hundreds/tens/ones
tricks.why: Working place-value by place-value avoids complicated borrowing when no borrowing is actually needed.

tricks.method: Add the right number of zeros: 34 × 100 = 3400.
tricks.why: Multiplying by 10 just shifts every digit one place value to the left - no calculation needed, just append zeros.

tricks.title: ×5 shortcut
tricks.why: 5 is exactly half of 10, so multiplying by 10 (easy) and halving (easy) is faster than direct ×5.

tricks.title: ×25 shortcut
tricks.why: 25 is a quarter of 100, so the multiplication becomes two very easy steps.

tricks.title: ×50 shortcut
tricks.why: 50 is half of 100, same idea as the ×5 trick but scaled up.

tricks.title: ×9 shortcut
tricks.why: 9 is just one less than 10, so multiplying by 10 and subtracting the original number once corrects for the difference.

tricks.title: ×11 pattern (2-digit numbers)
tricks.method: Add the two digits (3+4=7) and place the result between them: 374.
tricks.why: ×11 = ×10 + ×1, which for a 2-digit number always produces this 'add and insert' pattern (carry if the sum is 10 or more).

tricks.title: Doubling and halving
tricks.method: Halve 16 to 8, double 25 to 50: 8 × 50 = 400 (same answer as 16×25).
tricks.why: Halving one factor and doubling the other never changes the product, so you can trade an awkward multiplication for an easy one.

tricks.title: Near-100 multiplication
tricks.why: Expanding around a round base number turns a hard multiplication into simple round-number arithmetic.

tricks.title: ÷5 shortcut
tricks.why: Dividing by 5 is the same as doubling then dividing by 10 - both very fast mental steps.

tricks.title: ÷25 shortcut
tricks.why: This turns an awkward division into an easy multiplication followed by shifting the decimal point.

tricks.title: Factor division
tricks.when: Dividing by a number that factors nicely
tricks.why: Splitting the divisor into smaller factors turns one hard division into two easy ones.

tricks.title: Use known multiplication facts
tricks.why: Division is the reverse of multiplication, so a strong grip on times tables makes division instant.

tricks.title: 10% shortcut
tricks.why: Percent means 'out of 100', and 10 is one tenth of 100, so 10% is just one tenth of the number.

tricks.title: 5% shortcut
tricks.why: 5% is exactly half of 10%, so once you know the 10% trick, 5% is one more easy step.

tricks.title: 1% shortcut
tricks.why: 1% is literally one out of every hundred, so dividing by 100 gives it directly.

tricks.title: Build unusual percentages
tricks.why: Almost any percentage can be built by adding and subtracting easy building blocks like 10%, 5%, and 1%.

tricks.title: Find the unit fraction first
tricks.when: Calculating a fraction of a number
tricks.why: Breaking a fraction into 'one part' first, then scaling up, is far easier than trying to do it in one step.

tricks.title: Simplify early
tricks.when: Working with fractions in a calculation
tricks.method: Simplify 8/12 to 2/3 before continuing if possible - smaller numbers are easier to work with.
tricks.why: Simplifying as early as possible keeps the numbers small and reduces mistakes.

tricks.title: Common denominator method
tricks.method: Use 12 as a common denominator: 1/3=4/12, 1/4=3/12. Add: 7/12.
tricks.why: Fractions can only be added directly when they're counting the same-sized pieces - a common denominator makes that true.

tricks.title: Fraction/decimal/percentage conversion
tricks.method: 3/4 = 0.75 = 75%. Divide the numerator by the denominator to get the decimal, then ×100 for percent.
tricks.why: These are three ways of writing the exact same value - being fluent in converting between them makes many problems easier to approach.

tricks.title: Same-base multiplication
tricks.when: Multiplying powers with the same base
tricks.why: Multiplying powers of the same base just stacks more copies of that base together, which is why the exponents add.

tricks.title: Same-base division
tricks.when: Dividing powers with the same base
tricks.why: Dividing cancels out matching copies of the base, leaving only the difference in exponents.

tricks.title: Power of a power
tricks.when: Raising a power to another power
tricks.why: Raising to a power means repeating the multiplication that many times, which multiplies the exponents together.

tricks.title: Zero exponent
tricks.when: Any non-zero base to the power 0
tricks.why: Following the division rule backwards (a^n ÷ a^n = a^0 = 1) shows why anything divided by itself, expressed as exponents, must equal 1.

tricks.title: SOH CAH TOA
tricks.method: SOH: sin=Opposite/Hypotenuse. CAH: cos=Adjacent/Hypotenuse. TOA: tan=Opposite/Adjacent.
tricks.why: This classic mnemonic packs all three ratio definitions into one memorable phrase.

tricks.title: Angles on a line vs around a point
tricks.example: Angles on a line = 180°, around a point = 360°
tricks.method: A straight line is 'half a turn' (180°), a full point is 'one whole turn' (360°).
tricks.why: Thinking of angles as fractions of a full turn makes the 180°/360° facts intuitive instead of things to memorise blindly.

tricks.title: Z, F, C angle shapes
tricks.when: Parallel lines cut by a transversal
tricks.method: Z-shape = alternate angles (equal). F-shape = corresponding angles (equal). C-shape = co-interior angles (sum to 180°).
tricks.why: Spotting the letter shape in a diagram instantly tells you which angle rule applies.
